↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). PALESTINE originally denoted only the sea-coast of the land of Canaan inhabited by the Philistines (Exodus 15:14; Isaiah 14:29, 31; Joel 3:4), and in this sense exclusively the Hebrew name Pelesheth (rendered “Philistia” in Psalm 60:8; 83:7; 87:4; 108:9) occurs in the Old Testament. Not till a late period in Jewish history was this name used to denote “the land of the Hebrews” in general (Genesis 40:15). It is also called “the holy land” (Zechariah 2:12), the “land of Jehovah” (Hos. 9:3; Psalm 85:1), the “land of promise” (Hebrews 11:9), because promised to Abraham (Genesis 12:7; 24:7), the “land of Canaan” (Genesis 12:5), the “land of Israel” (1 Samuel 13:19), and the “land of Judah” (Isaiah 19:17). The territory promised as an inheritance to the seed of Abraham (Genesis 15:18-21; Numbers 34:1-12) was bounded on the east by the river Euphrates, on the west by the Mediterranean, on the north by the “entrance of Hamath,” and on the south by the “river of Egypt.” This extent of territory, about 60,000 square miles, was at length conquered by David, and was ruled over also by his son Solomon (2 Samuel 8; 1 Chronicles 18; 1 Kings 4:1, 21). This vast empire was the Promised Land; but Palestine was only a part of it, terminating in the north at the southern extremity of the Lebanon range, and in the south in the wilderness of Paran, thus extending in all to about 144 miles in length. Its average breadth was about 60 miles from the Mediterranean on the west to beyond the Jordan. It has fittingly been designated “the least of all lands.” Western Palestine, on the south of Gaza, is only about 40 miles in breadth from the Mediterranean to the Dead Sea, narrowing gradually toward the north, where it is only 20 miles from the sea-coast to the Jordan. Palestine, “set in the midst” (Ezekiel 5:5) of all other lands, is the most remarkable country on the face of the earth. No single country of such an extent has so great a variety of climate, and hence also of plant and animal life. Moses describes it as “a good land, a land of brooks of water, of fountains and depths that spring out of valleys and hills; a land of wheat, and barley, and vines, and fig trees, and pomegranates; a land of oil olive, and honey; a land wherein thou shalt not eat bread without scarceness, thou shalt not lack any thing in it; a land whose stones are iron, and out of whose hills thou mayest dig brass” (Deuteronomy 8:7-9). “In the time of Christ the country looked, in all probability, much as now. The whole land consists of rounded limestone hills, fretted into countless stony valleys, offering but rarely level tracts, of which Esdraelon alone, below Nazareth, is large enough to be seen on the map. The original woods had for ages disappeared, though the slopes were dotted, as now, with figs, olives, and other fruit-trees where there was any soil. Permanent streams were even then unknown, the passing rush of winter torrents being all that was seen among the hills. The autumn and spring rains, caught in deep cisterns hewn out like huge underground jars in the soft limestone, with artificial mud-banked ponds still found near all villages, furnished water. Hills now bare, or at best rough with stunted growth, were then terraced, so as to grow vines, olives, and grain. To-day almost desolate, the country then teemed with population. Wine-presses cut in the rocks, endless terraces, and the ruins of old vineyard towers are now found amidst solitudes overgrown for ages with thorns and thistles, or with wild shrubs and poor gnarled scrub” (Geikie’s Life of Christ). From an early period the land was inhabited by the descendants of Canaan, who retained possession of the whole land “from Sidon to Gaza” till the time of the conquest by Joshua, when it was occupied by the twelve tribes. Two tribes and a half had their allotments given them by Moses on the east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 3:12-20; comp. Numbers 1:17-46; Joshua 4:12-13). The remaining tribes had their portion on the west of Jordan. From the conquest till the time of Saul, about four hundred years, the people were governed by judges. For a period of one hundred and twenty years the kingdom retained its unity while it was ruled by Saul and David and Solomon. On the death of Solomon, his son Rehoboam ascended the throne; but his conduct was such that ten of the tribes revolted, and formed an independent monarchy, called the kingdom of Israel, or the northern kingdom, the capital of which was first Shechem and afterwards Samaria. This kingdom was destroyed. The Israelites were carried captive by Shalmanezer, king of Assyria, B.C. 722, after an independent existence of two hundred and fifty-three years. The place of the captives carried away was supplied by tribes brought from the east, and thus was formed the Samaritan nation (2 Kings 17:24-29). Nebuchadnezzar came up against the kingdom of the two tribes, the kingdom of Judah, the capital of which was Jerusalem, one hundred and thirty-four years after the overthrow of the kingdom of Israel. He overthrew the city, plundered the temple, and carried the people into captivity to Babylon (B.C. 587), where they remained seventy years. At the close of the period of the Captivity, they returned to their own land, under the edict of Cyrus (Ezra 1:1-4). They rebuilt the city and temple, and restored the old Jewish commonwealth. For a while after the Restoration the Jews were ruled by Zerubbabel, Ezra, and Nehemiah, and afterwards by the high priests, assisted by the Sanhedrin. After the death of Alexander the Great at Babylon (B.C. 323), his vast empire was divided between his four generals. Egypt, Arabia, Palestine, and Coele-Syria fell to the lot of Ptolemy Lagus. Ptolemy took possession of Palestine in B.C. 320, and carried nearly one hundred thousand of the inhabitants of Jerusalem into Egypt. He made Alexandria the capital of his kingdom, and treated the Jews with consideration, confirming them in the enjoyment of many privileges. After suffering persecution at the hands of Ptolemy’s successors, the Jews threw off the Egyptian yoke, and became subject to Antiochus the Great, the king of Syria. The cruelty and opression of the successors of Antiochus at length led to the revolt under the Maccabees (B.C. 163), when they threw off the Syrian yoke. In the year B.C. 68, Palestine was reduced by Pompey the Great to a Roman province. He laid the walls of the city in ruins, and massacred some twelve thousand of the inhabitants. He left the temple, however, unijured. About twenty-five years after this the Jews revolted and cast off the Roman yoke. They were however, subdued by Herod the Great (q.v.). The city and the temple were destroyed, and many of the inhabitants were put to death. About B.C. 20, Herod proceeded to rebuild the city and restore the ruined temple, which in about nine years and a half was so far completed that the sacred services could be resumed in it (comp. John 2:20). He was succeeded by his son Archelaus, who was deprived of his power, however, by Augustus, A.D. 6, when Palestine became a Roman province, ruled by Roman governors or procurators. Pontius Pilate was the fifth of these procurators. He was appointed to his office A.D. 25. Exclusive of Idumea, the kingdom of Herod the Great comprehended the whole of the country originally divided among the twelve tribes, which he divided into four provinces or districts. This division was recognized so long as Palestine was under the Roman dominion. These four provinces were, (1) Judea, the southern portion of the country; (2) Samaria, the middle province, the northern boundary of which ran along the hills to the south of the plain of Esdraelon; (3) Galilee, the northern province; and (4) Peraea (a Greek name meaning the “opposite country”), the country lying east of the Jordan and the Dead Sea. This province was subdivided into these districts, (1) Peraea proper, lying between the rivers Arnon and Jabbok; (2) Galaaditis (Gilead); (3) Batanaea; (4) Gaulonitis (Jaulan); (5) Ituraea or Auranitis, the ancient Bashan; (6) Trachonitis; (7) Abilene; (8) Decapolis, i.e., the region of the ten cities. The whole territory of Palestine, including the portions alloted to the trans-Jordan tribes, extended to about eleven thousand square miles. Recent exploration has shown the territory on the west of Jordan alone to be six thousand square miles in extent, the size of the principality of Wales.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SANCTUARY denotes, (1) the Holy Land (Exodus 15:17; comp. Psalm 114:2); (2) the temple (1 Chronicles 22:19; 2 Chronicles 29:21); (3) the tabernacle (Exodus 25:8; Leviticus 12:4; 21:12); (4) the holy place, the place of the Presence (Gr. hieron, the temple-house; not the naos, which is the temple area, with its courts and porches), Leviticus 4:6; Ephesians 2:21, R.V., marg.; (5) God’s holy habitation in heaven (Psalm 102:19). In the final state there is properly “no sanctuary” (Revelation 21:22), for God and the Lamb “are the sanctuary” (R.V., “temple”). All is there hallowed by the Divine Presence; all is sancturary.

Called nevi’ah (“prophetess”) here — only the second woman to receive that title in Hebrew scripture (after the unnamed mother of Isaiah’s sons in Isa 8:3 chronologically, but Miriam’s use is older textually). ↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Segullah (סְגֻלָּה) — “treasured possession.” The word denotes a private treasure of a king — items personally owned, distinct from the property of the realm. The term is used elsewhere of Israel only in Deut 7:6, 14:2, 26:18, and Mal 3:17 — always with the emphasis that the relation is personal and elective, not merely jurisdictional.

↩ ◇ Note. The Decalogue’s preamble. The Ten Commandments begin not with a command but with a self-identification: the God who liberated. This places the whole moral framework on a relational and historical basis — obedience flows from covenant rescue, not abstract duty. Rabbinic tradition counts this verse as the first “word” (dibbur) of the ten; most Christian traditions count starting from “no other gods.”

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I am the Lord thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage' — Ephrem reads the Pascal preface as the ground of every command that follows. The commandments are not arbitrary statutes but the rule-of-life of a delivered people; only the delivered are addressed by the Decalogue. Tewahedo catechesis preserves this priority of deliverance before commandment.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DECALOGUE the name given by the Greek fathers to the ten commandments; “the ten words,” as the original is more literally rendered (Exodus 20:3-17). These commandments were at first written on two stone slabs (31:18), which were broken by Moses throwing them down on the ground (32:19). They were written by God a second time (34:1). The decalogue is alluded to in the New Testament five times (Matthew 5:17, 18, 19; Mark 10:19; Luke 18:20; Romans 7:7, 8; 13:9; 1 Timothy 1:9, 10). These commandments have been divided since the days of Origen the Greek father, as they stand in the Confession of all the Reformed Churches except the Lutheran. The division adopted by Luther, and which has ever since been received in the Lutheran Church, makes the first two commandments one, and the third the second, and so on to the last, which is divided into two. “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s house” being ranked as ninth, and “Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour’s wife,” etc., the tenth. (See COMMANDMENTS.)

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Shabbat (שַׁבָּת) — to cease. The verb shavat means simply to stop, not “to rest” in the sense of recovery. The Sabbath commandment in Deuteronomy 5 grounds the day in liberation from slavery; here in Exodus 20 it is grounded in creation (Gen 2:2–3). The two rationales coexist throughout Israelite tradition: the day is at once cosmic and political — a weekly enactment of being a free creature in a created world.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy' — Ephrem reads Sabbath-rest as the canonical sign that creation is given a goal beyond labour: the Sabbath foreshadows the eighth-day rest of the Resurrection. Tewahedo alone among the major communions preserves both observances together — Saturday-Sabbath retained from Sinai and Sunday-Lord's-Day added from the Resurrection — and reads Ex 20:8 as the canonical anchor of the double observance.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Lo tirtzach (לֹא תִרְצָח). The verb ratzach denotes unlawful, personal killing — what English calls murder — not all forms of killing. The Hebrew Bible elsewhere uses different verbs (harag, hemit) for warfare and judicial execution, both of which the Torah continues to permit. Older English translations (KJV “thou shalt not kill”) blur this distinction; modern translations almost universally restore it.

↩ ◇ Note. The firstborn. The Passover institution turns the death of the firstborn (Exod 12) into a permanent claim on Israel’s firstborn — redeemed by substitute offering (13:13) or, for the priestly tribe, by Levite substitution (Num 3:12). Luke 2:23 cites this verse describing the presentation of Jesus at the Temple. The redemption-of-firstborn ceremony (pidyon ha-ben) on the thirty-first day of life remains a Jewish practice descending directly from this text.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SIN , WILDERNESS OF lying between Elim and sinai (Exodus 16:1; comp. Numbers 33:11, 12). This was probably the narrow plain of el-Markha, which stretches along the eastern shore of the Red Sea for several miles toward the promontory of Ras Mohammed, the southern extremity of the Sinitic Peninsula. While the Israelites rested here for some days they began to murmur on account of the want of nourishment, as they had by this time consumed all the corn they had brought with them out of Egypt. God heard their murmurings, and gave them “manna” and then quails in abundance.

↩ ◇ Note. Manna theology. The wilderness manna (described botanically in Num 11:7–9) is read as a sustained miracle of divine provision contingent on daily trust. Wisdom of Solomon 16:20 turns it into "food of angels"; John 6 has Jesus identifying himself as the true manna ("I am the bread of life"). The double-portion-on-Friday rule (16:5) embeds the Sabbath into the very logistics of survival — divine provisioning that itself rests.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HOBAB beloved, the Kenite, has been usually identified with Jethro (q.v.), Exodus 18:5, 27; comp. Numbers 10:29, 30. In Judges 4:11, the word rendered “father-in-law” means properly any male relative by marriage (comp. Genesis 19:14, “son-in-law,” A.V.), and should be rendered “brother-in-law,” as in the R.V. His descendants followed Israel to Canaan (Numbers 10:29), and at first pitched their tents near Jericho, but afterwards settled in the south in the borders of Arad (Judges 1:8-11, 16).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). JETHRO his excellence, or gain, a prince or priest of Midian, who succeeded his father Reuel. Moses spent forty years after his exile from the Egyptian court as keeper of Jethro’s flocks. While the Israelites were encamped at Sinai, and soon after their victory over Amalek, Jethro came to meet Moses, bringing with him Zipporah and her two sons. They met at the “mount of God,” and “Moses told him all that the Lord had done unto Pharaoh” (Exodus 18:8). On the following day Jethro, observing the multiplicity of the duties devolving on Moses, advised him to appoint subordinate judges, rulers of thousands, of hundreds, of fifties, and of tens, to decide smaller matters, leaving only the weightier matters to be referred to Moses, to be laid before the Lord. This advice Moses adopted (Exodus 18). He was also called Hobab (q.v.), which was probably his personal name, while Jethro was an official name. (See MOSES.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). APPEAL a reference of any case from an inferior to a superior court. Moses established in the wilderness a series of judicatories such that appeals could be made from a lower to a higher (Exodus 18:13-26.) Under the Roman law the most remarkable case of appeal is that of Paul from the tribunal of Festus at Caesarea to that of the emperor at Rome (Acts 25:11, 12, 21, 25). Paul availed himself of the privilege of a Roman citizen in this matter.

↩ ◇ Note. Jethro’s counsel. A non-Israelite priest of Midian gives Moses governance advice — and Moses takes it. The narrative is theologically generous: wisdom can come from outside the covenant community. The system Jethro proposes (chiefs of thousands, hundreds, fifties, tens) becomes the template for Israelite judicial administration. The Qumran community’s organizational documents (1QS) draw on this same passage for their hierarchical structure.

↩ ◇ Note. The first commandment. The Hebrew ‘al panai ("before/beside my face") admits two readings: monolatry (Yahweh alone among existing gods is to be worshipped) or strict monotheism (no other gods exist). Most modern scholarship reads early Israelite religion as monolatrous, with explicit monotheism crystallizing later (Isaiah 40–55). The Decalogue’s grammar fits the monolatrous reading more naturally; the systematic monotheism becomes explicit in Deuteronomy and the prophets.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). THEFT Punished by restitution, the proportions of which are noted in 2 Samuel 12:6. If the thief could not pay the fine, he was to be sold to a Hebrew master till he could pay (Exodus 22:1-4). A night-thief might be smitten till he died, and there would be no blood-guiltiness for him (22:2). A man-stealer was to be put to death (21:16). All theft is forbidden (Exodus 20:15; 21:16; Leviticus 19:11; Deuteronomy 5:19; 24:7; Psalm 50:18; Zechariah 5:3; Matthew 19:18; Romans 13:9; Ephesians 4:28; 1 Peter 4:15).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEAST This word is used of flocks or herds of grazing animals (Exodus 22:5; Numbers 20:4, 8, 11; Psalm 78:48); of beasts of burden (Genesis 45:17); of eatable beasts (Proverbs 9:2); and of swift beasts or dromedaries (Isaiah 60:6). In the New Testament it is used of a domestic animal as property (Revelation 18:13); as used for food (1 Corinthians 15:39), for service (Luke 10:34; Acts 23:24), and for sacrifice (Acts 7:42). When used in contradistinction to man (Psalm 36:6), it denotes a brute creature generally, and when in contradistinction to creeping things (Leviticus 11:2-7; 27:26), a four-footed animal. The Mosaic law required that beasts of labour should have rest on the Sabbath (Exodus 20:10; 23:12), and in the Sabbatical year all cattle were allowed to roam about freely, and eat whatever grew in the fields (Exodus 23:11; Leviticus 25:7). No animal could be castrated (Leviticus 22:24). Animals of different kinds were to be always kept separate (Leviticus 19:19; Deuteronomy 22:10). Oxen when used in threshing were not to be prevented from eating what was within their reach (Deuteronomy 25:4; 1 Corinthians 9:9). This word is used figuratively of an infuriated multitude (1 Corinthians 15:32; Acts 19:29; comp. Psalm 22:12, 16; Ecclesiastes 3:18; Isaiah 11:6-8), and of wicked men (2 Peter 2:12). The four beasts of Daniel 7:3, 17, 23 represent four kingdoms or kings.

↩ ◇ Note. The alien protection laws. The motivation clause is unusual in ancient Near Eastern law: not a command from royal authority, but appeal to shared experience ("you were aliens in Egypt"). This formulation appears 36+ times in the Pentateuch — making protection of the foreigner one of the most repeated commandments in Torah. The same logic recurs in Deut 10:19 and Lev 19:33–34 ("love him as yourself"), where the foreigner becomes a paradigm-case for the love commandment.

It is supposed to have been obtained from a shellfish of the Mediterranean, the Helix ianthina of Linnaeus. The robe of the high priest’s ephod was to be all of this colour (Exodus 28:31), also the loops of the curtains (26:4) and the ribbon of the breastplate (28:28). Blue cloths were also made for various sacred purposes (Numbers 4:6, 7, 9, 11, 12). (See COLOUR.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ACACIA (Hebrews shittim) Exodus 25:5, R.V. probably the Acacia seyal (the gum-arabic tree); called the “shittah” tree (Isaiah 41:19). Its wood is called shittim wood (Exodus 26:15,26; 25:10,13,23,28, etc.). This species (A. seyal) is like the hawthorn, a gnarled and thorny tree. It yields the gum-arabic of commerce. It is found in abundance in the Sinaitic peninsula.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BADGER this word is found in Exodus 25:5; 26:14; 35:7, 23; 36:19; 39:34; Numbers 4:6, etc. The tabernacle was covered with badgers’ skins; the shoes of women were also made of them (Ezekiel 16:10). Our translators seem to have been misled by the similarity in sound of the Hebrew tachash and the Latin taxus, “a badger.” The revisers have correctly substituted “seal skins.” The Arabs of the Sinaitic peninsula apply the name tucash to the seals and dugongs which are common in the Red Sea, and the skins of which are largely used as leather and for sandals. Though the badger is common in Palestine, and might occur in the wilderness, its small hide would have been useless as a tent covering. The dugong, very plentiful in the shallow waters on the shores of the Red Sea, is a marine animal from 12 to 30 feet long, something between a whale and a seal, never leaving the water, but very easily caught. It grazes on seaweed, and is known by naturalists as Halicore tabernaculi.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. V’shakhanti b’tokham (וְשָׁכַנְתִּי בְּתוֹכָם). The verb shakhan ("dwell, tabernacle") generates the noun mishkan (tabernacle) and the later rabbinic shekhinah (the indwelling presence). John 1:14 ("the Word became flesh and dwelt — eskēnōsen, tabernacled — among us") deliberately echoes this verse via the LXX. The verse establishes the central theological claim of the second half of Exodus: God’s purpose in delivering Israel from Egypt is dwelling among them.

↩ ◇ Note. Moses’ Levite genealogy. The narrative opens Moses’ story without naming his parents — Amram and Jochebed are named only later (6:20). The deliberate anonymity heightens the sense that this child arrives without context, found rather than born into rank. The detail that both parents are Levites is theologically loaded: Moses comes from the tribe that will, by the end of Exodus, be set apart for sanctuary service.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. ’Ehyeh asher ’ehyeh (אֶהְיֶה אֲשֶׁר אֶהְיֶה). The most famous verbal puzzle in the Hebrew Bible. The verb hayah ("to be") is in the first-person imperfect, which can render as: "I am that I am," "I will be what I will be," "I am the one who is," "I cause to be what is." The LXX gives egō eimi ho ōn ("I am the One who is"), influencing all subsequent Greek-philosophical reading of God as Being itself. Maimonides took the Hebrew as denoting necessary existence; Ricoeur as fidelity-promise; Buber as presence ("I shall be present"). The form connects to the divine name YHWH (also from the root h-y-h).

↩ ◇ Note. The Bridegroom of Blood. One of the strangest passages in the Pentateuch. As Moses is en route to Egypt — having just been commissioned — God attacks him at a night encampment. Zipporah saves him by circumcising her son and touching Moses’s feet with the blood, declaring "a bridegroom of blood you are to me." The episode foreshadows Passover: blood of circumcision saves Moses, blood of the lamb saves Israel.

↩ ◇ Note. Pesaḥ (פֶּסַח). The verb pasaḥ, source of the festival name, occurs in v.13 ("I will pass over") and probably means "to limp," "to skip," or "to spare." The festival meal is to be eaten standing, dressed for travel — eternalizing the urgency of the Exodus night. The Christian Eucharist takes its institution from this meal (Mark 14:12–25). The Ethiopian Tewahedo Church preserves a strong Passover-Eucharist link in its liturgy.

↩ ◇ Note. Tefillin. Together with Deut 6:8 and 11:18, this verse is the basis for the Jewish practice of binding scriptural texts in small leather cases on the arm and head. The literal interpretation became normative; the Karaites later argued for a metaphorical reading. The phrase "a memorial between your eyes" gives the head-tefillin its place; "a sign on your hand" gives the arm-tefillin its place. Pharisaic-rabbinic literalism here vs. spiritualizing readings represents one of the deepest interpretive divergences in Second Temple Judaism.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Israel passes through the sea on dry ground with the waters as a wall on either hand. Paul reads this as 'baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea' (1 Cor 10:2); Ephrem follows Paul and reads Ex 14:22 as the founding scriptural figure of Christian baptism. Tewahedo carries this as the principal OT type of its baptismal liturgy: the people pass through the waters and emerge a people.

↩ ✦ Topic. Topics. This verse appears under: EGYPT, EGYPTIANS, MANASSEH, NAPHTALI, REUBEN, SIMEON, ZEBULUN, MANASSEH, NAPHTALI, REUBEN, SIMEON, ZEBULUN, MIRACLES.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RED SEA , PASSAGE OF The account of the march of the Israelites through the Red Sea is given in Exodus 14:22-31. There has been great diversity of opinion as to the precise place where this occurred. The difficulty of arriving at any definite conclusion on the matter is much increased by the consideration that the head of the Gulf of Suez, which was the branch of the sea that was crossed, must have extended at the time of the Exodus probably 50 miles farther north than it does at present. Some have argued that the crossing took place opposite the Wady Tawarik, where the sea is at present some 7 miles broad. But the opinion that seems to be best supported is that which points to the neighbourhood of Suez. This position perfectly satisfies all the conditions of the stupendous miracle as recorded in the sacred narrative. (See EXODUS.)

↩ ◇ Note. The Sea of Reeds. The Hebrew yam suf is traditionally translated "Red Sea" via the LXX, but "Reed Sea" is closer to the Hebrew. Likely refers to a marshy lake region in the eastern Nile delta. The miracle is described differently in different sources within the chapter: a strong east wind drying the sea (14:21 — naturalistic), water as walls (14:22 — supernatural). Both readings are kept side by side in the canonical text.

↩ ◇ Note. The Song of the Sea. Exodus 15 is one of the oldest poetic strata of the Hebrew Bible (alongside Judges 5, the Song of Deborah). Its archaic Hebrew, parallelism, and triumphal celebration of God-as-warrior preserves a martial theology that later prophetic and wisdom traditions will both honor and complicate. The Ethiopian Tewahedo liturgy still incorporates this song. The image of God as warrior is uncomfortable for many modern readers; the Bible itself wrestles with it (cf. Isa 2:4, the swords-into-plowshares).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). MERIBAH quarrel or strife. (1.) One of the names given by Moses to the fountain in the desert of Sin, near Rephidim, which issued from the rock in Horeb, which he smote by the divine command, “because of the chiding of the children of Israel” (Exodus 17:1-7). It was also called Massah (q.v.). It was probably in Wady Feiran, near Mount Serbal. (2.) Another fountain having a similar origin in the desert of Zin, near to Kadesh (Numbers 27:14). The two places are mentioned together in Deuteronomy 33:8. Some think the one place is called by the two names (Psalm 81:7). In smiting the rock at this place Moses showed the same impatience as the people (Numbers 20:10-12). This took place near the close of the wanderings in the desert (Numbers 20:1-24; Deuteronomy 32:51).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). REPHIDIM supports, one of the stations of the Israelites, situated in the Wady Feiran, near its junction with the Wady esh-Sheikh. Here no water could be found for the people to drink, and in their impatience they were ready to stone Moses, as if he were the cause of their distress. At the command of God Moses smote “the rock in Horeb,” and a copious stream flowed forth, enough for all the people. After this the Amalekites attacked the Israelites while they were here encamped, but they were utterly defeated (Exodus 17:1, 8-16). They were the “first of the nations” to make war against Israel (Numbers 24:20). Leaving Rephidim, the Israelites advanced into the wilderness of Sinai (Exodus 19:1, 2; Numbers 33:14, 15), marching probably through the two passes of the Wady Solaf and the Wady esh-Sheikh, which converge at the entrance to the plain er-Rahah, the “desert of Sinai,” which is two miles long and about half a mile broad. (See SINAI; MERIBAH.)

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (365). Ephrem the Syrian Hymns on the Crucifixion (c. 365 AD)

The rock struck by Moses' rod pours out water for the thirsty people, and Ephrem joins Paul (1 Cor 10:4) in reading the rock as Christ. The striking is the Crucifixion; the water is the Spirit and the eucharistic stream (Jn 19:34 — blood and water from the pierced side). Tewahedo treats Ex 17:6 and Jn 19:34 as a single canonical disclosure of the smitten Christ releasing the rivers of living water.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). SINAI of Sin (the moon God), called also Horeb, the name of the mountain district which was reached by the Hebrews in the third month after the Exodus. Here they remained encamped for about a whole year. Their journey from the Red Sea to this encampment, including all the windings of the route, was about 150 miles. The last twenty-two chapters of Exodus, together with the whole of Leviticus and Numbers ch. 1-11, contain a record of all the transactions which occurred while they were here. From Rephidim (Exodus 17:8-13) the Israelites journeyed forward through the Wady Solaf and Wady esh-Sheikh into the plain of er-Rahah, “the desert of Sinai,” about 2 miles long and half a mile broad, and encamped there “before the mountain.” The part of the mountain range, a protruding lower bluff, known as the Ras Sasafeh (Sufsafeh), rises almost perpendicularly from this plain, and is in all probability the Sinai of history. Dean Stanley thus describes the scene:, “The plain itself is not broken and uneven and narrowly shut in, like almost all others in the range, but presents a long retiring sweep, within which the people could remove and stand afar off. The cliff, rising like a huge altar in front of the whole congregation, and visible against the sky in lonely grandeur from end to end of the whole plain, is the very image of the ‘mount that might be touched,’ and from which the voice of God might be heard far and wide over the plain below.” This was the scene of the giving of the law. From the Ras Sufsafeh the law was proclaimed to the people encamped below in the plain of er-Rahah. During the lengthened period of their encampment here the Israelites passed through a very memorable experience. An immense change passed over them. They are now an organized nation, bound by covenant engagement to serve the Lord their God, their ever-present divine Leader and Protector. At length, in the second month of the second year of the Exodus, they move their camp and march forward according to a prescribed order. After three days they reach the “wilderness of Paran,” the “et-Tih”, i.e., “the desert”, and here they make their first encampment. At this time a spirit of discontent broke out amongst them, and the Lord manifested his displeasure by a fire which fell on the encampment and inflicted injury on them. Moses called the place Taberah (q.v.), Numbers 11:1-3. The journey between Sinai and the southern boundary of the Promised Land (about 150 miles) at Kadesh was accomplished in about a year. (See MAP facing page 204.)

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

When Moses lifted up his hands Israel prevailed against Amalek; when he let them down Amalek prevailed. Ephrem reads the cruciform posture as the secret of the victory: Moses' arms outstretched are the Cross fore-figured, and the war is won not by the sword in the valley but by the cross-shape on the hill. Tewahedo carries this as the canonical OT type of Christian intercessory prayer in the cross-posture.

↩ ◇ Note. The lifted hands. Moses’s upraised arms — held up by Aaron and Hur — became one of early Christianity’s most-cited typologies of the Cross (already in the Epistle of Barnabas 12; later in Justin, Tertullian, Augustine). The Ethiopian Tewahedo iconographic tradition preserves the same reading. Independent of the typology, the narrative is clear: the battle’s fortunes follow the prayer-posture, not the military skill.

↩ ◇ Note. Mamleket kohanim (מַמְלֶכֶת כֹּהֲנִים). The corporate priesthood of Israel — every member a priest before the nations. 1 Peter 2:9 applies the same phrase to the Church. The democratization of priesthood is one of Israel’s distinctive contributions to ancient religious thought; in surrounding ANE cultures, priesthood was a royal-administrative class. Israel inverts: the whole people is mediator.

↩ ◇ Note. The First Commandment. "Before me" (‘al panay) more literally "in my presence" or "to my face." Some scholars distinguish monolatry (worshipping one God while granting others exist) from monotheism (denying others exist) — and read this commandment as monolatry, with monotheism developing later (Deut 4:35, Isa 44:6). The classical Jewish and Christian reading, however, takes the commandment as already implicitly monotheistic.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BASIN or Bason. (1.) A trough or laver (Hebrews aggan’) for washing (Exodus 24:6); rendered also “goblet” (Cant. 7:2) and “cups” (Isaiah 22:24). (2.) A covered dish or urn (Hebrews k’for) among the vessels of the temple (1 Chronicles 28:17; Ezra 1:10; 8:27). (3.) A vase (Hebrews mizrak) from which to sprinkle anything. A metallic vessel; sometimes rendered “bowl” (Amos 6:6; Zechariah 9:15). The vessels of the tabernacle were of brass (Exodus 27:3), while those of the temple were of gold (2 Chronicles 4:8). (4.) A utensil (Hebrews saph) for holding the blood of the victims (Exodus 12:22); also a basin for domestic purposes (2 Samuel 17:28). The various vessels spoken of by the names “basin, bowl, charger, cup, and dish,” cannot now be accurately distinguished. The basin in which our Lord washed the disciples’ feet (John 13:5) must have been larger and deeper than the hand-basin.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant meal. One of the most extraordinary passages in scripture: the seventy elders "see God" and eat with him on the mountain. The text immediately notes God did not lay a hand on them — i.e., they survived the encounter. The pavement of sapphire under God’s feet later becomes a stock image in apocalyptic literature (Ezek 1:26). The communal meal in God’s presence prefigures Eucharistic theology.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'Let them make me a sanctuary; that I may dwell among them' — Ephrem reads this verse as the canonical warrant for every consecrated dwelling-place of God: the tabernacle prefigures the Incarnation ('the Word was made flesh and tabernacled among us,' Jn 1:14), and the Incarnation prefigures the Church. Tewahedo cites Ex 25:8 as the principal canonical anchor of its tabot tradition — the Ark-as-sanctuary at the center of every Tewahedo church.

The whole tabernacle theology of Exodus is reread Christologically through this single verb.

↩ ◇ Note. Pharaoh’s question. Pharaoh’s "Who is Yahweh?" is the theological problem the rest of the book is going to answer. The Egyptian king’s question is asked from a polytheistic premise — he assumes Yahweh is one tribal deity among many — and the entire plague sequence is structured as an extended answer: Yahweh is the one whose power demonstrably surpasses every Egyptian deity (Hapi the Nile-god in plague 1, Heqet the frog-goddess in plague 2, etc.; cf. 12:12, "I will execute judgments against all the gods of Egypt"). The narrative is theologically self-conscious: the question Pharaoh asks ironically becomes the structuring rhetorical question of the next ten chapters. By 9:27 Pharaoh confesses "Yahweh is righteous"; by 12:31 he commands the exodus he initially refused. The narrative architecture is deliberately catechetical — the king who did not know Yahweh learns through plague, and the reader learns alongside him.

↩ ◇ Note. The Israelite foremen’s complaint. The Israelite foremen, beaten by Pharaoh’s slave-drivers because the people cannot meet the increased brick-quota, turn on Moses and Aaron with bitter accusation: their advocacy has made things worse. The episode is the first of many in which Israel itself becomes Moses’ opposition — a pattern that will run through the wilderness narratives and become the deuteronomistic theme of "stiff-necked" Israel. The verse is also psychologically realistic about how oppression frequently turns the oppressed against their advocates rather than the oppressors: when liberation produces immediate worsening before improvement, the advocates become the visible cause of the suffering. The narrative refuses to romanticize the people Moses is leading; it consistently shows them as ungrateful, frightened, and shortsighted. The honesty is theologically programmatic — Yahweh does not redeem Israel because Israel deserves redemption but because Yahweh has made covenant promises that bind even when the recipients are unworthy.

↩ ◇ Note. The Egyptian magicians. Pharaoh’s court magicians replicate the first plagues with their latim ("secret arts"), then fail at the gnats (8:18) and confess "this is the finger of God." Egyptian magical literature (the Demotic Magical Papyri, Coffin Texts) confirms the historical reality of the priestly-magical class the text portrays. Jewish tradition names two of them, Yannes and Yambres (cited in 2 Tim 3:8), expanding the narrative through pseudepigraphic literature.

↩ ◇ Note. The plague-distinction principle. Beginning here (in plague 5, the cattle-pestilence) and intensifying through plagues 6–10, the narrative consistently distinguishes Egyptian from Israelite suffering: only Egyptian livestock die, only Egypt experiences darkness (10:23), only Egyptian firstborn perish (12:29–30). The principle — Yahweh making "a distinction" (palah, 11:7) between Egyptian and Israelite — frames the exodus as judicial-discriminating action rather than indiscriminate plague. Theologically it answers the question why Israelites were not affected: not because they were geographically separate (Goshen is not far from Egyptian population centers) but because Yahweh’s judgment is targeted. The Passover ritual of ch 12 will operationalize the same principle at the family level: blood on the doorpost makes the household a discriminated zone. The exodus narrative’s entire theological logic — judgment against Egypt, deliverance for Israel — depends on this principle of discriminating divine action.

↩ ◇ Note. "For this purpose I have raised you up." The verse is one of the OT’s most theologically charged formulations of divine sovereignty over human history: Pharaoh’s very existence as Egyptian king is portrayed as instrumental to Yahweh’s revelation. Paul cites this verse explicitly at Rom 9:17 in his sustained meditation on divine election, sovereignty, and human responsibility — making it one of the foundational texts for the entire Christian theological tradition on predestination. Augustine, Calvin, and Aquinas all engage Rom 9 (and through it this verse) at length; Pelagius, Erasmus, and Arminius read it differently. The OT verse itself is deliberately vivid — Yahweh has not just permitted Pharaoh’s recalcitrance but has positioned the king "for this purpose." The same divine sovereignty over an opposing king’s heart will recur in Cyrus (Isa 45:1, "Yahweh’s anointed") and even Nebuchadnezzar (Jer 25:9, "my servant"). The verse encodes one of the OT’s most uncompromising formulations of the deity’s control over human political action.

↩ ◇ Note. The locust plague. Locusts (Heb. arbeh) were the most feared agricultural disaster in the ANE — a single swarm could consume the food supply of a regional population. Egyptian sources confirm the destructive potential: the Famine Stela of the Ptolemaic era retrojects locust catastrophes onto Djoser’s reign as the worst-imaginable catastrophe; Ugaritic and Mesopotamian texts treat locust swarms as divine punishment by default. The plague’s theological significance: it strikes Egypt’s remaining agriculture after the hail of plague 7, depriving Pharaoh’s court of food — the chapter is the OT’s clearest articulation of plagues working in cumulative economic logic. Joel 1–2 takes the locust plague as the prophetic image of Yahweh’s eschatological "Day of the Lord," developing the Exodus pattern into apocalyptic vocabulary. The verse’s superlative formula ("never were there such locusts before, nor shall there be again") is part of the chapter’s deliberate intensification — each plague exceeds the last.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). RED SEA The sea so called extends along the west coast of Arabia for about 1,400 miles, and separates Asia from Africa. It is connected with the Indian Ocean, of which it is an arm, by the Strait of Bab-el-Mandeb. At a point (Ras Mohammed) about 200 miles from its nothern extremity it is divided into two arms, that on the east called the AElanitic Gulf, now the Bahr el-‘Akabah, about 100 miles long by 15 broad, and that on the west the Gulf of Suez, about 150 miles long by about 20 broad. This branch is now connected with the Mediterranean by the Suez Canal. Between these two arms lies the Sinaitic Peninsula. The Hebrew name generally given to this sea is Yam Suph. This word suph means a woolly kind of sea-weed, which the sea casts up in great abundance on its shores. In these passages, Exodus 10:19; 13:18; 15:4, 22; 23:31; Numbers 14:25, etc., the Hebrew name is always translated “Red Sea,” which was the name given to it by the Greeks. The origin of this name (Red Sea) is uncertain. Some think it is derived from the red colour of the mountains on the western shore; others from the red coral found in the sea, or the red appearance sometimes given to the water by certain zoophytes floating in it. In the New Testament (Acts 7:36; Hebrews 11:29) this name is given to the Gulf of Suez. This sea was also called by the Hebrews Yam-mitstraim, i.e., “the Egyptian sea” (Isaiah 11:15), and simply Ha-yam, “the sea” (Exodus 14:2, 9, 16, 21, 28; Joshua 24:6, 7; Isaiah 10:26, etc.). The great historical event connected with the Red Sea is the passage of the children of Israel, and the overthrow of the Egyptians, to which there is frequent reference in Scripture (Exodus 14, 15; Numbers 33:8; Deuteronomy 11:4; Joshua 2:10; Judges 11:16; 2 Samuel 22:16; Nehemiah 9:9-11; Psalm 66:6; Isaiah 10:26; Acts 7:36, etc.).

↩ ◇ Note. The ninth plague. The three days of palpable darkness — Hebrew "darkness which may be felt" (yamesh ḥoshekh) — is the most cosmically pointed of the plagues: it directly attacks Ra, the Egyptian sun-god and supreme deity of the New Kingdom pantheon. The Egyptian theology of kingship rested on the Pharaoh’s identification with Ra’s son and the Pharaoh’s preservation of the cosmic order against the encroaching darkness. This plague reverses that order: darkness reigns over Egypt while the Israelites in Goshen have light (10:23). The plague functions as the immediate prelude to the climactic plague of the firstborn — Egyptian theology’s sun-god having been demonstrably overcome, the Pharaoh’s own status as Ra’s son will be the next target. The Wisdom of Solomon (17:2–18:4) develops the verse into an elaborate meditation on the spiritual darkness of Egypt’s injustice contrasted with the light of Israel’s deliverance. The plague is the theological hinge of the cycle.

↩ ◇ Note. The firstborn judgment. The threatened final plague targets the firstborn male of every Egyptian household — from Pharaoh’s royal heir to the firstborn of household servants, plus the firstborn of livestock. The targeting is theologically precise: "Israel is my firstborn son" (4:22), and Pharaoh’s refusal to release Yahweh’s firstborn is now answered by the death of Egypt’s firstborns. The principle — measure for measure (middah k’neged middah in later rabbinic vocabulary) — is one of the OT’s recurrent theological-judicial frameworks. The Passover ritual of ch 12 functions as the Israelite firstborn’s ransom: blood on the doorpost substitutes for the firstborn’s death, grounding the OT theology of substitutionary atonement that later Christian thought (especially Heb 9–10) develops Christologically. The verse is the structural pivot of the entire exodus narrative — the plague that Pharaoh cannot withstand, that produces the immediate release.

↩ ◇ Note. The silence of the dogs. The detail — not a single dog will growl during the firstborn plague — registers the absolute supernatural quiet that will accompany the night of the angel of death’s passage through Egypt. The image is precise and chilling: in any normal night-event of mass death, dogs across the city would bark in chorus; the silence is the signature of divinely calibrated judgment. Egyptian dogs were associated with Anubis, the jackal-headed god of the dead — the silent dogs may be a small, pointed signal that Anubis himself has been overcome, that the Egyptian death-pantheon is paralyzed during the very night Yahweh visits Egypt with death. The detail also belongs to the chapter’s broader pattern of distinguishing Israel from Egypt: Israel’s livestock and people will be silent and unaffected, only Egypt will hear the cry of universal lamentation (12:30, "a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead"). The contrast of cosmic noise against absolute silence is the chapter’s most striking literary effect.

↩ ◇ Note. The Song of the Sea. One of the oldest preserved poems in Hebrew, datable on linguistic grounds to the late second millennium BCE — quite possibly older than the prose narrative that introduces it. Its archaic forms (yqtl tense usage, enclitic mem, infrequent definite article) are diagnostic. The song closes with Yahweh enthroned forever (15:18) — possibly the earliest royal-cosmic-kingship statement in the Bible. The Mishnah (Pesachim 10) lists this song as part of the Hallel sung at Passover.

FREEDOM The law of Moses pointed out the cases in which the servants of the Hebrews were to receive their freedom (Exodus 21:2-4, 7, 8; Leviticus 25:39-42, 47-55; Deuteronomy 15:12-18). Under the Roman law the “freeman” (ingenuus) was one born free; the “freedman” (libertinus) was a manumitted slave, and had not equal rights with the freeman (Acts 22:28; comp. Acts 16:37-39; 21:39; 22:25; 25:11, 12).

↩ ◇ Note. The pierced-ear ceremony. The provision concerns the Hebrew slave whose six-year term has ended (cf. 21:2) but who chooses, out of love for his master’s family, to remain a permanent member of the household: he is brought to "God" (the household tribunal, or the local sanctuary) and his ear is pierced against the doorpost as a permanent mark. The ceremony combines several theological registers: the doorway as threshold of household identity (cf. 12:7, the Passover blood on doorposts), the ear as the organ of obedience (cf. Pss 40:6–8, "ears you have dug for me," cited Christologically at Heb 10:5–7), and the irreversible mark of permanent commitment. Paul’s self-designation as "slave of Christ Jesus" (Rom 1:1, Phil 1:1) draws on the same conceptual world — the freed person who chooses lifelong service. The Hebrew slave-law generally is one of the OT’s remarkable institutions: a worker is enslaved for at most six years, with the seventh year as automatic release (21:2) — far more humane than most ANE slave-codes.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CONCUBINE in the Bible denotes a female conjugally united to a man, but in a relation inferior to that of a wife. Among the early Jews, from various causes, the difference between a wife and a concubine was less marked than it would be amongst us. The concubine was a wife of secondary rank. There are various laws recorded providing for their protection (Exodus 21:7; Deuteronomy 21:10-14), and setting limits to the relation they sustained to the household to which they belonged (Genesis 21:14; 25:6). They had no authority in the family, nor could they share in the household government. The immediate cause of concubinage might be gathered from the conjugal histories of Abraham and Jacob (Genesis 16;30). But in process of time the custom of concubinage degenerated, and laws were made to restrain and regulate it (Exodus 21:7-9). Christianity has restored the sacred institution of marriage to its original character, and concubinage is ranked with the sins of fornication and adultery (Matthew 19:5-9; 1 Corinthians 7:2).

↩ ◇ Note. Lex talionis at Sinai. The first occurrence of the talion formula in the Pentateuch (also Lev 24:20, Deut 19:21). In its ANE legal context, the formula functions as a limit on retaliation: punishment must be proportional, never excessive. Hammurabi §§196–197 includes literal mutilations as the realized form; Hebrew rabbinic interpretation (Mekhilta on Exodus 21, b. Bava Kamma 83b–84a) understood the formula from the start as referring to monetary compensation calibrated to lost function rather than literal mutilation. Whether the rabbinic reading reflects original intent or interpretive softening is debated; literal mutilation is rare in actual Jewish legal practice. Jesus’ "you have heard it said… but I say to you" (Matt 5:38–39) does not abolish the proportionality limit but transcends it: refuse retaliation entirely. The verse is one of the most consistently misunderstood OT texts in popular reception — read as license for revenge when the original purpose was the opposite.

↩ ◇ Note. The alien-protection clause. One of the OT’s most-repeated commands, occurring in slightly varying forms more than thirty times across the Pentateuch and prophets (cf. Lev 19:33–34, Deut 10:19, 24:14–22, Jer 7:6, Zech 7:10, Mal 3:5). The grounding rationale here is experiential: "you know the heart of an alien, since you were aliens in the land of Egypt." The provision uses Israel’s own historical trauma as the moral foundation for treatment of immigrants — Israel knows what it feels like to be a foreigner mistreated, and that knowledge becomes covenantal obligation. The principle is one of the OT’s clearest examples of empathy-based ethics: the experience of suffering is to be converted into the policy of refusing to inflict that same suffering on others. The contemporary political resonance is sharp; the provision has been a major reference point in modern Jewish and Christian advocacy for refugee and immigrant protection. Few OT verses have so direct an application across such a long stretch of legal-political history.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). BEG That the poor existed among the Hebrews we have abundant evidence (Exodus 23:11; Deuteronomy 15:11), but there is no mention of beggars properly so called in the Old Testament. The poor were provided for by the law of Moses (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 12:12; 14:29). It is predicted of the seed of the wicked that they shall be beggars (Psalm 37:25; 109:10). In the New Testament we find not seldom mention made of beggars (Mark 10:46; Luke 16:20, 21; Acts 3:2), yet there is no mention of such a class as vagrant beggars, so numerous in the East. “Beggarly,” in Galatians 4:9, means worthless.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HANNAH favour, grace, one of the wives of Elkanah the Levite, and the mother of Samuel (1 Samuel 1; 2). Her home was at Ramathaim-zophim, whence she was wont every year to go to Shiloh, where the tabernacle had been pitched by Joshua, to attend the offering of sacrifices there according to the law (Exodus 23:15; 34:18; Deuteronomy 16:16), probably at the feast of the Passover (comp. Exodus 13:10). On occasion of one of these “yearly” visits, being grieved by reason of Peninnah’s conduct toward her, she went forth alone, and kneeling before the Lord at the sanctuary she prayed inaudibly. Eli the high priest, who sat at the entrance to the holy place, observed her, and misunderstanding her character he harshly condemned her conduct (1 Samuel 1:14-16). After hearing her explanation he retracted his injurious charge and said to her, “Go in peace: and the God of Israel grant thee thy petition.” Perhaps the story of the wife of Manoah was not unknown to her. Thereafter Elkanah and his family retired to their quiet home, and there, before another Passover, Hannah gave birth to a son, whom, in grateful memory of the Lord’s goodness, she called Samuel, i.e., “heard of God.” After the child was weaned (probably in his third year) she brought him to Shiloh into the house of the Lord, and said to Eli the aged priest, “Oh my Lord, I am the woman that stood by thee here, praying unto the Lord. For this child I prayed; and the Lord hath given me my petition which I asked of him: therefore I also have granted him to the Lord; as long as he liveth he is granted to the Lord” (1 Samuel 1:27, 28, R.V.). Her gladness of heart then found vent in that remarkable prophetic song (2:1-10; comp. Luke 1:46-55) which contains the first designation of the Messiah under that name (1 Samuel 2:10, “Annointed” = “Messiah”). And so Samuel and his parents parted. He was left at Shiloh to minister “before the Lord.” And each year, when they came up to Shiloh, Hannah brought to her absent child “a little coat” (Hebrews meil, a term used to denote the “robe” of the ephod worn by the high priest, Exodus 28:31), a priestly robe, a long upper tunic (1 Chronicles 15:27), in which to minister in the tabernacle (1 Samuel 2:19; 15:27; Job 2:12). “And the child Samuel grew before the Lord.” After Samuel, Hannah had three sons and two daughters.

↩ ◇ Note. The first occurrence of the kid-in-milk prohibition. The verse appears three times in the Pentateuch (here, 34:26, Deut 14:21) — a triple attestation that, in rabbinic interpretation (b. Hullin 113b), generates the threefold separation of meat from milk in kashrut: not cooking together, not eating together, not benefiting from the mixture. The literal practice the verse forbids is documented in 14th-century-BCE Ugaritic ritual texts (KTU 1.23, the "Birth of the Gracious Gods"), where boiling a kid in milk appears as a Canaanite ritual gesture — making the verse a pointed prohibition of a specific known pagan rite. The rabbinic generalization is therefore an interpretive expansion well beyond the literal sense, but the literal sense itself is precisely calibrated: avoid the cultic practice of the surrounding peoples. The verse is one of the OT’s most striking examples of how a single ritual prohibition can generate an entire dietary tradition.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LORD There are various Hebrew and Greek words so rendered. (1.) Hebrews Jehovah, has been rendered in the English Bible LORD, printed in small capitals. This is the proper name of the God of the Hebrews. The form “Jehovah” is retained only in Exodus 6:3; Psalm 83:18; Isaiah 12:2; 26:4, both in the Authorized and the Revised Version. (2.) Hebrews ‘adon, means one possessed of absolute control. It denotes a master, as of slaves (Genesis 24:14, 27), or a ruler of his subjects (45:8), or a husband, as Lord of his wife (18:12). The old plural form of this Hebrew word is ’adonai. From a superstitious reverence for the name “Jehovah,” the Jews, in reading their Scriptures, whenever that name occurred, always pronounced it ’Adonai. (3.) Greek kurios, a supreme master, etc. In the LXX. this is invariably used for “Jehovah” and “‘Adonai.” (4.) Hebrews ba’al, a master, as having domination. This word is applied to human relations, as that of husband, to persons skilled in some art or profession, and to heathen deities. “The men of Shechem,” literally “the baals of Shechem” (Judges 9:2, 3). These were the Israelite inhabitants who had reduced the Canaanites to a condition of vassalage (Joshua 16:10; 17:13). (5.) Hebrews seren, applied exclusively to the “lords of the Philistines” (Judges 3:3). The LXX. render it by satrapies. At this period the Philistines were not, as at a later period (1 Samuel 21:10), under a kingly government. (See Joshua 13:3; 1 Samuel 6:18.) There were five such lordships, viz., Gath, Ashdod, Gaza, Ashkelon, and Ekron.

↩ ◇ Note. The covenant formula. The verse is one of the OT’s clearest articulations of the so-called "covenant formula" — the bilateral commitment "I will be your God, and you shall be my people" (cf. Lev 26:12, Jer 7:23, 11:4, 24:7, 30:22, 31:33, Ezek 11:20, 36:28, 37:23, 27, Zech 8:8). The formula compresses the entire substance of covenantal relationship into a single bidirectional clause: divine self-commitment to be Israel’s God, Israel’s self-commitment to be Yahweh’s people. The formula’s eschatological development at Rev 21:3 ("the dwelling of God is with men, and they will be his people") makes it one of the canonical bookends of biblical theology — appearing here at Israel’s formation and recurring at the consummation of all things. The chapter places the formula within Yahweh’s response to Israel’s discouragement (cf. 5:21–6:1) — covenant identity is asserted precisely when the covenant partners cannot yet feel it.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). ENCHANTMENTS (1.) The rendering of Hebrew latim or lehatim, which means “something covered,” “muffled up;” secret arts, tricks (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7, 18), by which the Egyptian magicians imposed on the credulity of Pharaoh. (2.) The rendering of the Hebrew keshaphim, “muttered spells” or “incantations,” rendered “sorceries” in Isaiah 47:9, 12, i.e., the using of certain formulae under the belief that men could thus be bound. (3.) Hebrew lehashim, “charming,” as of serpents (Jeremiah 8:17; comp. Psalm 58:5). (4.) Hebrew nehashim, the enchantments or omens used by Balaam (Numbers 24:1); his endeavouring to gain omens favourable to his design. (5.) Hebrew heber (Isaiah 47:9, 12), “magical spells.” All kinds of enchantments were condemned by the Mosaic law (Leviticus 19:26; Deuteronomy 18:10-12). (See DIVINATION.)

↩ ◇ Note. The "you shall know" refrain. The phrase "you shall know that I am Yahweh" (Hebrew vidatem ki ani Adonai) recurs as the structuring rhetorical refrain of the plague narratives (cf. 7:5, 8:10, 8:22, 9:14, 9:29, 10:2, 14:4, 14:18) and becomes one of Ezekiel’s most distinctive formulas — the prophet uses it more than 70 times across his book. Its theological function is precise: the plagues are not just punishment but pedagogy, delivering knowledge of Yahweh to Egyptians, Israelites, and the surrounding nations. The verse establishes the principle that divine action is inherently revelatory — Yahweh acts in history not just to accomplish ends but to make himself known. The principle becomes one of the load-bearing premises of OT theology, with prophetic-historical action consistently framed as divine self-disclosure rather than as bare power-assertion. The verse is theologically the most concentrated single line in plague 1.

↩ ◇ Note. The frog plague. Heqet, the Egyptian frog-headed goddess, was associated with childbirth and fertility — the swarming frogs of plague 2 directly target an Egyptian deity. The plague’s theological precision matches the pattern of the cycle: each plague disables a specific Egyptian deity (Hapi the Nile-god in plague 1, Heqet here, Geb the earth-god in plague 3, Khepri the scarab-god in plague 4, etc.). The plague is also unique in that Pharaoh’s magicians can replicate it (8:7) but cannot stop it — they can multiply frogs but cannot remove them. The detail is psychologically devastating: the magicians’ "success" only worsens the catastrophe. Ps 78:45 and 105:30 commemorate the plague specifically. The chapter’s opening verses also encode a wordplay: the Hebrew "frog" (tzefarde‘a) appears in the singular collectively (8:6, "the frog covered the land of Egypt"), giving the impression of one massive amphibian-blanket rather than discrete creatures.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

'I will rain bread from heaven for you' — the manna of the wilderness is for Ephrem the direct prophetic anchor of Jn 6: 'I am the bread which came down from heaven.' The wilderness bread sustains the body for a day; the Eucharist sustains the soul for eternity. Tewahedo Anaphora cites Ex 16:4 and Jn 6 together as the OT-NT diptych of the eucharistic gift.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CLOUD The Hebrew so rendered means “a covering,” because clouds cover the sky. The word is used as a symbol of the Divine presence, as indicating the splendour of that glory which it conceals (Exodus 16:10; 33:9; Numbers 11:25; 12:5; Job 22:14; Psalm 18:11). A “cloud without rain” is a proverbial saying, denoting a man who does not keep his promise (Proverbs 16:15; Isaiah 18:4; 25:5; Jude 1:12). A cloud is the figure of that which is transitory (Job 30:15; Hos. 6:4). A bright cloud is the symbolical seat of the Divine presence (Ex.29:42, 43; 1 Kings 8:10; 2 Chronicles 5:14; Ezekiel 43:4), and was called the Shechinah (q.v.). Jehovah came down upon Sinai in a cloud (Exodus 19:9); and the cloud filled the court around the tabernacle in the wilderness so that Moses could not enter it (Exodus 40:34, 35). At the dedication of the temple also the cloud “filled the house of the Lord” (1 Kings 8:10). Thus in like manner when Christ comes the second time he is described as coming “in the clouds” (Matthew 17:5; 24:30; Acts 1:9, 11). False teachers are likened unto clouds carried about with a tempest (2 Peter 2:17). The infirmities of old age, which come one after another, are compared by Solomon to “clouds returning after the rain” (Ecclesiastes 12:2). The blotting out of sins is like the sudden disappearance of threatening clouds from the sky (Isaiah 44:22). Cloud, the pillar of, was the glory-cloud which indicated God’s presence leading the ransomed people through the wilderness (Exodus 13:22; 33:9, 10). This pillar preceded the people as they marched, resting on the ark (Exodus 13:21; 40:36). By night it became a pillar of fire (Numbers 9:17-23).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CAMP During their journeys across the wilderness, the twelve tribes formed encampments at the different places where they halted (Exodus 16:13; Numbers 2:3). The diagram here given shows the position of the different tribes and the form of the encampment during the wanderings, according to Numbers 1:53; 2:2-31; 3:29, 35, 38; 10:13-28. The area of the camp would be in all about 3 square miles. After the Hebrews entered Palestine, the camps then spoken of were exclusively warlike (Joshua 11:5, 7; Judges 5:19, 21; 7:1; 1 Samuel 29:1; 30:9, etc.).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). QUAILS The Israelites were twice relieved in their privation by a miraculous supply of quails, (1) in the wilderness of Sin (Exodus 16:13), and (2) again at Kibroth-hattaavah (q.v.), Numbers 11:31. God “rained flesh upon them as dust, and feathered fowls like as the sand of the sea” (Psalm 78:27). The words in Numbers 11:31, according to the Authorized Version, appear to denote that the quails lay one above another to the thickness of two cubits above the ground. The Revised Version, however, reads, “about two cubits above the face of the earth”, i.e., the quails flew at this height, and were easily killed or caught by the hand. Being thus secured in vast numbers by the people, they “spread them all abroad” (11:32) in order to salt and dry them. These birds (the Coturnix vulgaris of naturalists) are found in countless numbers on the shores of the Mediterranean, and their annual migration is an event causing great excitement.

↩ ⌘ Hebrew. Man hu (מָן הוּא). The Israelites’ question on first seeing the desert food — "What is it?" (man hu) — becomes the food’s permanent name: man, "manna." The text is doing folk-etymology, but with theological intent: the food’s name encodes Israel’s ignorance about it. The Hebrew preserves the puzzlement: this is not bread, not flesh, not anything Israel has a vocabulary for. The substance is described botanically (16:31, "like coriander seed, white, with the taste of wafers made with honey") but never identified — which is the point. Manna is engineered to be theologically useful in its physical inexplicability. Jesus’ "I am the bread of life" discourse in John 6 (especially 6:31–58) takes this verse as central type — the bread that comes down from heaven, that supplies inexplicably, becomes Christological figure. Heb 9:4 records that a jar of manna was preserved inside the ark as one of three sacred memorials (with the rod and the tablets). The verse is the OT root of one of the most theologically productive food-images in biblical tradition.

↩ ◇ Note. The rock at Horeb. The first water-from-the-rock episode (cf. the second at Num 20:8–13, where Moses’ disobedience costs him the land). Paul cites this rock at 1 Cor 10:4 in one of the NT’s most striking typological readings: "they drank from the spiritual rock that followed them, and that rock was Christ." The rabbinic tradition Paul draws on (cf. Tosefta Sukkah 3:11) imagines the rock literally accompanying Israel through the wilderness as a perpetual water-source; Paul takes the tradition and Christologizes it. The chapter’s placement of the episode at "Horeb" (the alternate name for Sinai) is geographically suggestive — the very mountain of covenant-giving will turn out to be the site of water-from-rock. The episode also generates a place-name pun: "Massah" (testing) and "Meribah" (quarreling), 17:7 — Israel’s wilderness skepticism materialized as toponym. The verse opens one of the OT’s richest typological clusters in the entire Pentateuch.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FOREIGNER a Gentile. Such as resided among the Hebrews were required by the law to be treated with kindness (Exodus 22:21; 23:9; Leviticus 19:33, 34; 23:22; Deuteronomy 14:28; 16:10, 11; 24:19). They enjoyed in many things equal rights with the native-born residents (Exodus 12:49; Leviticus 24:22; Numbers 15:15; 35:15), but were not allowed to do anything which was an abomination according to the Jewish law (Exodus 20:10; Leviticus 17:15,16; 18:26; 20:2; 24:16, etc.).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). LOAN The Mosaic law required that when an Israelite needed to borrow, what he asked was to be freely lent to him, and no interest was to be charged, although interest might be taken of a foreigner (Exodus 22:25; Deuteronomy 23:19, 20; Leviticus 25:35-38). At the end of seven years all debts were remitted. Of a foreigner the loan might, however, be exacted. At a later period of the Hebrew commonwealth, when commerce increased, the practice of exacting usury or interest on loans, and of suretiship in the commercial sense, grew up. Yet the exaction of it from a Hebrew was regarded as discreditable (Psalm 15:5; Proverbs 6:1, 4; 11:15; 17:18; 20:16; 27:13; Jeremiah 15:10). Limitations are prescribed by the law to the taking of a pledge from the borrower. The outer garment in which a man slept at night, if taken in pledge, was to be returned before sunset (Exodus 22:26, 27; Deuteronomy 24:12, 13). A widow’s garment (Deuteronomy 24:17) and a millstone (6) could not be taken. A creditor could not enter the house to reclaim a pledge, but must remain outside till the borrower brought it (10, 11). The Hebrew debtor could not be retained in bondage longer than the seventh year, or at farthest the year of jubilee (Exodus 21:2; Leviticus 25:39, 42), but foreign sojourners were to be “bondmen for ever” (Leviticus 25:44-54).

↩ ◇ Note. The blasphemy-and-ruler clause. The verse couples two prohibitions: cursing God and cursing a ruler (Hebrew nasi, "leader, prince"). The pairing assumes a theology of derivative authority — the ruler’s legitimacy participates in divine authority, and cursing the ruler is therefore cognate with cursing God. Paul cites this verse at Acts 23:5 (apologizing to the high priest Ananias whom Paul has rebuked: "I did not know, brothers, that he was high priest; for it is written, ‘You shall not speak evil of a ruler of your people’"). The passage’s NT use is theologically significant: Paul, even when correctly accusing the high priest of judicial corruption, treats the verse as binding on his own speech. The verse’s narrower legal effect in OT context concerns courtroom speech — false accusation, public cursing, defamatory speech against community leaders — and connects to the broader OT prohibitions on perjury and false witness. The chapter is one of the OT’s clearest treatments of speech-acts as legally consequential.

↩ ◇ Note. The blood of the covenant. Moses splashes half the sacrificial blood on the altar and half on the people, formally inaugurating the Sinai covenant. The phrase "the blood of the covenant" (Hebrew dam ha-b’rit) becomes one of the most theologically charged in scripture: Jesus deliberately echoes it at the Last Supper ("this is my blood of the covenant," Matt 26:28, Mark 14:24, Luke 22:20, 1 Cor 11:25), framing the eucharist as the new analog to the Sinai blood-rite. Heb 9:18–22 makes the parallel explicit: the OT covenant required blood, the new covenant is similarly inaugurated with blood. The detail of the chapter — Moses sprinkling half on the altar (Yahweh’s side) and half on the people (the human partners) — encodes a theology of covenantal binding through shared substance. Few OT rituals have so directly shaped subsequent Christian sacramental theology and liturgical language. The chapter is the institutional and theological foundation of every later "blood of the covenant" formulation in the canon.

↩ ◇ Note. The Jethro reform. The verse codifies one of the OT’s most institutionally consequential reorganizations: Moses’ father-in-law Jethro, a Midianite priest (and therefore a non-Israelite), advises Moses to delegate ordinary judicial cases to a hierarchical structure of judges over 1,000s, 100s, 50s, and 10s — keeping only the difficult cases for himself. The pattern recurs in Israelite military and judicial organization through the rest of the OT (Deut 1:15, 1 Sam 22:7, 2 Kgs 1:9–14). The provision’s narrative significance is theological: the institutional design Yahweh’s people will use is brought into Israel by a Midianite outsider, and Yahweh’s people accept it. The chapter quietly acknowledges that wisdom from outside Israel can legitimately shape Israelite institutions — a stance importantly different from the conquest-rhetoric of separation that dominates other parts of the Pentateuch. Jethro’s blessing (18:10–12) is also unusual: a non-Israelite priest pronounces benedictions over Yahweh’s deeds and offers sacrifice with Aaron and the elders. The chapter is one of the OT’s most positive portraits of religious-cultural exchange.

↩ ◇ Ephrem the Syrian (360). Ephrem the Syrian Commentary on Exodus (c. 360 AD)

Pharaoh's edict that every male Hebrew infant be cast into the river is, for Ephrem, the first scriptural sign of Mastema-mirror tyranny: the murderous power decrees the very fate it will suffer. The plague of the firstborn and the Red Sea reverse Pharaoh's decree on his own house. Tewahedo reads this as the canonical pattern by which oppressor measures are returned upon oppressors.

'I will take you to me for a people, and I will be to you a God' — Ephrem hears in this verse the completion of the Abrahamic-Isaac-Jacob promise: the patriarchal seed becomes a peoplehood under a single covenanted Name. ↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). AARON the eldest son of Amram and Jochebed, a daughter of Levi (Exodus 6:20). Some explain the name as meaning mountaineer, others mountain of strength, illuminator. He was born in Egypt three years before his brother Moses, and a number of years after his sister Miriam (2:1,4; 7:7). He married Elisheba, the daughter of Amminadab of the house of Judah (6:23; 1 Chronicles 2:10), by whom he had four sons, Nadab and Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. When the time for the deliverance of Isarael out of Egypt drew nigh, he was sent by God (Exodus 4:14,27-30) to meet his long-absent brother, that he might co-operate with him in all that they were required to do in bringing about the Exodus. He was to be the “mouth” or “prophet” of Moses, i.e., was to speak for him, because he was a man of a ready utterance (7:1,2,9,10,19). He was faithful to his trust, and stood by Moses in all his interviews with Pharaoh. When the ransomed tribes fought their first battle with Amalek in Rephidim, Moses stood on a hill overlooking the scene of the conflict with the rod of God in his outstretched hand. On this occasion he was attended by Aaron and Hur, his sister’s husband, who held up his wearied hands till Joshua and the chosen warriors of Israel gained the victory (17:8-13). Afterwards, when encamped before Sinai, and when Moses at the command of God ascended the mount to receive the tables of the law, Aaron and his two sons, Nadab and Abihu, along with seventy of the elders of Israel, were permitted to accompany him part of the way, and to behold afar off the manifestation of the glory of Israel’s God (Exodus 19:24; 24:9-11). While Moses remained on the mountain with God, Aaron returned unto the people; and yielding through fear, or ignorance, or instability of character, to their clamour, made unto them a golden calf, and set it up as an object of worship (Exodus 32:4; Psalm 106:19). On the return of Moses to the camp, Aaron was sternly rebuked by him for the part he had acted in this matter; but he interceded for him before God, who forgave his sin (Deuteronomy 9:20). On the mount, Moses received instructions regarding the system of worship which was to be set up among the people; and in accordance therewith Aaron and his sons were consecrated to the priest’s office (Leviticus 8; 9). Aaron, as high priest, held henceforth the prominent place appertaining to that office. When Israel had reached Hazeroth, in “the wilderness of Paran,” Aaron joined with his sister Miriam in murmuring against Moses, “because of the Ethiopian woman whom he had married,” probably after the death of Zipporah. But the Lord vindicated his servant Moses, and punished Miriam with leprosy (Numbers 12). Aaron acknowledged his own and his sister’s guilt, and at the intercession of Moses they were forgiven. Twenty years after this, when the children of Israel were encamped in the wilderness of Paran, Korah, Dathan, and Abiram conspired against Aaron and his sons; but a fearful judgment from God fell upon them, and they were destroyed, and the next day thousands of the people also perished by a fierce pestilence, the ravages of which were only stayed by the interposition of Aaron (Numbers 16). That there might be further evidence of the divine appointment of Aaron to the priestly office, the chiefs of the tribes were each required to bring to Moses a rod bearing on it the name of his tribe. And these, along with the rod of Aaron for the tribe of Levi, were laid up overnight in the tabernacle, and in the morning it was found that while the other rods remained unchanged, that of Aaron “for the house of Levi” budded, blossomed, and yielded almonds (Numbers 17:1-10). This rod was afterwards preserved in the tabernacle (Hebrews 9:4) as a memorial of the divine attestation of his appointment to the priesthood. Aaron was implicated in the sin of his brother at Meribah (Numbers 20:8-13), and on that account was not permitted to enter the Promised Land. When the tribes arrived at Mount Hor, “in the edge of the land of Edom,” at the command of God Moses led Aaron and his son Eleazar to the top of that mountain, in the sight of all the people. There he stripped Aaron of his priestly vestments, and put them upon Eleazar; and there Aaron died on the top of the mount, being 123 years old (Numbers 20:23-29. Comp. Deuteronomy 10:6; 32:50), and was “gathered unto his people.” The people, “even all the house of Israel,” mourned for him thirty days. Of Aaron’s sons two survived him, Eleazar, whose family held the high-priesthood till the time of Eli; and Ithamar, in whose family, beginning with Eli, the high-priesthood was held till the time of Solomon. Aaron’s other two sons had been struck dead (Leviticus 10:1,2) for the daring impiety of offering “strange fire” on the alter of incense. The Arabs still show with veneration the traditionary site of Aaron’s grave on one of the two summits of Mount Hor, which is marked by a Mohammedan chapel. His name is mentioned in the Koran, and there are found in the writings of the rabbins many fabulous stories regarding him. He was the first anointed priest. His descendants, “the house of Aaron,” constituted the priesthood in general. In the time of David they were very numerous (1 Chronicles 12:27). The other branches of the tribe of Levi held subordinate positions in connection with the sacred office. Aaron was a type of Christ in his official character as the high priest. His priesthood was a “shadow of heavenly things,” and was intended to lead the people of Israel to look forward to the time when “another priest” would arise “after the order of Melchizedek” (Hebrews 6:20). (See MOSES.)
